extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, journalism students, media critics, and general readers interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for ethical photojournalism — what counts as responsible, accurate, and non-exploitative practice in press photography, especially conflict/war reporting. Emphasises honesty in representation, avoidance of sensationalism, and institutional accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain absolute objectivity and ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute objectivity and ethical standards need to be upheld by photojournalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the 'disease of sensationalism and fabrication'. Treat the camera's power responsibly; photography should inform, inspire, and influence positively rather than mislead. Institutions must enforce ethical behaviour rather than rely solely on market incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not manipulate images to change their meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs must not be altered in ways that change their meaning or present a darker/more damaging version of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include enlarging/enhancing smoke, cloning buildings, or altering a defensive flare to appear as a missile (Adnan Hajj examples). Such alterations are unacceptable because they fabricate a new contradiction/shock factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit editing to aesthetic improvements only
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Photoshop for slight changes in colouring and lighting to improve photos is acceptable, but altering content or meaning is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between permissible adjustments (colour, exposure, lighting) and impermissible manipulations (adding/cloning elements, darkening to change perceived menace). Editors should set clear boundaries for acceptable post-processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify staging and subject identity; avoid publishing staged propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers and news organizations must verify whether scenes are staged and confirm the identities/roles of subjects before publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Green Helmet Man' was presented as a rescue worker but was later shown to be Salam Daher, an actor/director of propaganda. Failure to verify can result in publishing pro-jihadist propaganda or otherwise misleading material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exploiting suffering and voyeuristic sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Photojournalism should not exploit victims' suffering for shock value or profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses the Kevin Carter controversy where critics argued he profited from suffering instead of intervening. The author argues against cynical dismissal but insists on a duty comparable to professions that 'maintain the health of society's conscious' — i.e., responsibility to minimize exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use images as blackmail or coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Images should not be used as tools of blackmail or to coerce audiences; the audience-attracting power of scandal must not be weaponised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes that photographs' attention-grabbing power has been used as blackmail and warns against this practice in both tabloid and mainstream media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fanning the flames of war or warmongering for profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Media must not publish or amplify images in ways that intentionally escalate conflict or act as warmongering for financial/gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adnan Hajj's doctored images are criticised as potentially exacerbating conflicts; the author equates morally dubious media practices with culpability similar to arms dealers when imagery contributes to violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions must investigate and hold staff accountable after ethical breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulation or staging is exposed, news organisations should scrutinise the implicated photographer's broader body of work and take appropriate disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Reuters placed Hajj's other photos under scrutiny and terminated his employment after alterations were revealed. The author calls for 'serious action' beyond exposure by bloggers or citizen journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers should perform due diligence rather than rely solely on syndication or trust
rubrics_metrics.description: News organisations and editors should not simply accept freelance submissions at face value; they owe readers verification and fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticises Reuters for failing to detect doctored images and implies editors must implement verification processes to prevent dissemination of manipulated imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen journalists and bloggers are important for accountability but cannot be the only remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Bloggers and citizen journalists can reveal misconduct (as in the Hajj case) but systemic institutional fixes are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the blogosphere exposed the alterations, the author stresses that 'serious action needs to be taken' by formal institutions to extinguish exploitation, especially when lives are at stake.
